synthesis.headline: Blocked ridge-cutoff dipole holds into a fourth day: Labor Day heat dome anchors the midsection while a deepening southeast-Canada trough drives Great Lakes-to-Mid-Atlantic severe and a Northeast cool-down
synthesis.narrative:
The high-amplitude, blocked longwave pattern Tlaloc has tracked all week is still the organizing story, now in its fourth-plus day. The DuPage 500 mb analysis reads the same three-part structure: a cutoff low (560-564 dam) over the Pacific Northwest and interior British Columbia, a strongly amplified ridge (588-594 dam) arcing from the central Rockies and southern Plains into the Great Lakes and Ontario, and an eastern trough (570-576 dam) over the Ohio Valley and Mid-Atlantic. As the summaries correctly note, the western anticyclone sits equatorward and east of the cutoff rather than poleward of it, so this is an amplified ridge-cutoff dipole, not a true Rex block. The flow is decidedly blocked rather than progressive, and the practical consequence is a heat dome anchored over the midsection through the Labor Day weekend — WPC advertises major to extreme heat with widespread Heat Advisories and Extreme Heat Warnings — with the action, as usual, living on the flanks of the ridge.

Today's focal points line up on those flanks. The severe threat is a Slight Risk from the southern Great Lakes through the Mid-Atlantic, tied to a cluster/MCS moving southeast out of the upper Midwest into the diurnally destabilizing Ohio Valley; damaging outflow winds are the primary concern, with the best overlap of shear and buoyancy over central and eastern Ohio and bowing segments expected. This is driven by the upper trough deepening over southeastern Canada, which is also steering a genuine cool air mass into the Northeast — temperatures dropping into the 40s-50s by Sunday morning. The heavy-rain headlines are secondary but real: monsoonal moisture over Arizona and New Mexico carries a Slight Risk of excessive rainfall along the AZ-NM border, and weak disturbances keep the Gulf Coast and Florida vulnerable to flash flooding within the deep tropical moisture that the Air Mass RGB shows blanketing the entire Southeast and Gulf. In Canada, the western baroclinic zone has shifted north relative to yesterday: the deep BC/Yukon low has retreated toward the Alaska-Yukon border (about 986 hPa) and a stout 1031 hPa high has built over interior western Canada, tightening the gradient and focusing lift across the Prairie provinces on the high's northern and western flanks.

The upper-level context ties it together and answers the regime question. The broad red-orange plume on the Air Mass RGB from the central Rockies across the southern Plains into the lower Mississippi Valley is warm, dry, low-PV air on the anticyclonic side of the ridge — the heat and convective suppression there come from subsidence, midlevel warming, and capping, not from the modest surface highs beneath. The sharp orange-to-green transition running from the Texas Panhandle toward the Ohio Valley marks the jet corridor and airmass boundary, and impulses along it feed the northern-stream severe. On whether the southeast-Canada trough is disrupting the heat regime: the ensemble pair says no — this is geographic contraction, not collapse. The Day 2 outlook confirms the eastern shortwave is progressive, sweeping the severe threat southeast to the central Appalachians and Carolinas Saturday behind a southward-advancing front while substantial ridging still sits over the Plains. Comparing the 6-10 day (Sep 9-13) to the 8-14 day (Sep 11-17), the western ridge keeps retreating: the zero anomaly line already lies near the Pacific coast at 6-10 days with more zonal flow offshore, and by 8-14 days there is no positive-anomaly ridge over the northern Rockies or northern Plains at all — the ridge axis has slid to the Desert Southwest and northern Mexico (576-582 dam) with only a weak downstream bump over Kansas-Oklahoma, all while a deep polar low anchors the Canadian Arctic. That is the classic ridge-retreat-toward-the-Southwest signature: the southern tier stays hot, the northern tier trends cooler and more active. The weakly negative and falling PNA and the positive, rising AO are directionally consistent with fading western ridging and reduced high-latitude blocking, but as weak summer signals they serve only as a lagging cross-check on the height and PV fields.
synthesis.climate_context: This is peak-season North America running close to script for early September under a developing El Niño. The ONI table shows the basin having warmed from weak La Niña (about -0.6 C late 2025) to moderate El Niño by summer 2026 (+1.80 in JJA), and the tropics fit that state precisely: a crowded East Pacific carrying three simultaneous hurricanes (Karina, Lowell, Marie) plus a 50 percent chance of another system developing well offshore southwestern Mexico next week, set against a suppressed Atlantic where — at the climatological hurricane-season peak — no development is expected anywhere for seven days. The North American Monsoon remains active, driving daily Southwest and high-terrain convection with the excessive-rainfall risk along the AZ-NM border. Severe weather is expressing itself in the expected late-summer mode — ridge-periphery, northern-stream and frontal storms across the Great Lakes, Ohio Valley, and Appalachians rather than deep-Plains outbreaks — while the dominant domestic climate signal remains the durable, dangerous central-U.S. heat now peaking over the Labor Day weekend.
synthesis.regional_notes: SPC has an active mesoscale discussion for the organizing MCS over eastern Wisconsin, which may intensify as it crosses into lower Michigan and potentially Ohio/Indiana overnight, with severe wind gusts (55-70 mph) and hail to 1.25 inches; low-level warm advection and a 30-40 kt jet are strengthening the cold pool, and watch issuance is possible but uncertain (40 percent). On Day 2 the same system's remnants may re-fire from the lower Ohio Valley toward the WV/VA mountains, with an isolated large-hail and wind threat also over the northern/central Plains. Localized flash-flood risk runs from the Arizona-New Mexico border into the Southwest on monsoon moisture, with additional Gulf Coast and Florida flash-flood potential. Along the western Canadian gradient between the 1031 hPa interior high and the Alaska-Yukon low, a cold front crossing interior BC/Alberta supports a focused band of lift and wind across the Prairies. Worth flagging again: Air Mass imagery shows a cyclonically curved higher-PV streamer near the Yucatan Channel and convective swirls over the Greater Antilles and western Atlantic, yet NHC expects no Atlantic development for seven days — a satellite/outlook discrepancy that has now persisted several days.

sources.title: Surface Analysis
sources.summary: This 0900Z 4 September 2026 WPC surface analysis shows a sprawling low pressure complex across the interior West, with centers readable near 1001 mb over the central Rockies and a secondary around 1005 mb over the southern Plains, consistent with late-summer thermal trough activity rather than a dynamically deep system. A 1013 mb high sits over the Desert Southwest and a 1017-1018 mb high is positioned over the southeastern United States, neither particularly strong for the season. The most prominent frontal activity is a cold front draped from the northern Rockies southeastward toward the central Plains, with what appears to be a stationary or slow-moving segment extending further east across the Ohio Valley; a warm front is also apparent across portions of the northern tier from the upper Midwest toward the Great Lakes. Pressure gradient is tightest along and immediately behind the cold front from the northern High Plains into the central Rockies, where isobars are visibly compressed, implying meaningful post-frontal winds in that corridor; gradients are notably slack across the southeastern quadrant of the country under the broad ridge. The frontal zone across the central Plains to Great Lakes, combined with the low center and confluent wind observations shown in the station data, marks the primary surface focus for lift and moisture convergence, with dewpoints in the upper 60s to mid 70s F evident in station plots from the Gulf Coast northward into the Mississippi Valley, supporting convective potential in the prefrontal air mass.

sources.title: Canadian Surface Analysis
sources.summary: This CMC surface analysis valid 0000Z Friday 04 September 2026 shows Hurricane Karina centered near 20.0N 138.0W over the eastern tropical Pacific, well south of the Mexican coast and posing no immediate direct threat to Canada, though its moisture field may eventually interact with midlatitude flow. Over the Canadian domain proper, the dominant feature is a broad high centered near 1031 hPa situated over what appears to be the interior of western Canada or the northern Rockies corridor, with its isobars connecting southward into a 1023 hPa high over the central or southern Plains; the tight gradient on the high's northern and western flanks, where isobars pack against a frontal boundary trailing westward, would support a focused band of lift and wind across the Canadian Prairie provinces. A low of approximately 986 hPa sits over what the chart geometry places in the vicinity of Alaska or the Yukon-Alaska border region, with a cold front extending southeastward and likely crossing into interior British Columbia or Alberta, though the projection makes the precise provincial crossing ambiguous; station models along that boundary show backing winds and higher dewpoints on the warm side. In the upper portion of the frame, several lows in the 985-1005 hPa range are distributed across the Arctic Ocean and the high Arctic archipelago, ordinary for the polar basin, and should not be read as continental Canadian systems. Across eastern Canada the gradient is comparatively relaxed under the influence of a high near 1016-1024 hPa over the central Atlantic and Great Lakes region, suggesting a period of quieter conditions from Ontario eastward through Quebec and the Maritimes on this chart time.

sources.title: 500 mb Analysis
sources.summary: The 500 mb pattern at 1200 UTC 4 September 2026 shows a high-amplitude longwave configuration with a deep western trough centered over the Pacific Northwest and interior British Columbia, where heights fall to around 560-564 dam and a closed low is depicted, indicating a cutoff feature that is no longer embedded in the progressive westerlies. Downstream, a pronounced ridge axis extends from the central Rockies and southern Plains northeastward into the Great Lakes and Ontario region, with heights reaching 588-594 dam across the ridge core; this ridge is strongly amplified and appears to be retarding eastward progression of the upstream cutoff. The eastern trough is evident over the Ohio Valley and Mid-Atlantic, where heights drop back to roughly 570-576 dam, giving the pattern a classic Rex-like appearance over the West in the sense of a cutoff low juxtaposed against the amplified ridge immediately to its east, though the anticyclone center is displaced equatorward and eastward rather than poleward of the low, so a true Rex block geometry is not met — more accurately this is an amplified ridge-cutoff dipole. The green shading indicating wind speeds highlights two implied jet corridors: one wrapping cyclonically around the western cutoff over the Pacific Northwest into Canada, and a second streak across the northeastern United States and the western Atlantic where height gradients are tightest, consistent with a 115-knot or greater jet maximum near New England. The overall flow is decidedly blocked rather than progressive, with the cutoff low over the Northwest likely pivoting slowly rather than translating, and the surface low plotted over the Gulf Coast region sitting beneath the eastern trough axis in a position consistent with cyclogenetic forcing.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB (GOES-19)
sources.summary: This GOES-19 Air Mass RGB from 04 September 2026 at 13:21Z shows a broad red-orange plume of dry upper-tropospheric air arching from the central Rockies eastward across the southern Plains and into the lower Mississippi Valley, consistent with the anticyclonic side of a mid-level ridge rather than a stratospheric intrusion. The sharpest color transition — from orange-red to green — runs roughly along a southwest-to-northeast line from the Texas Panhandle toward the Ohio Valley, marking the implied jet corridor and likely airmass boundary separating that dry air to the northwest from deeper tropical moisture to the south and east. A compact but vivid orange-red streamer with a more elongated, cyclonically curved appearance wraps around a feature over the central Gulf of Mexico near the Yucatan Channel area, where it pinches against bright white convective tops; this geometry is more consistent with a trough or weak cutoff on the cyclonic-shear side of the flow and merits closer inspection as a possible higher-PV dry intrusion. Organized deep convection with cold white tops is visible over the upper Midwest near the Illinois-Wisconsin border, along the Mid-Atlantic coast, and in a separate cluster over the Greater Antilles and western Atlantic, where a discrete swirl of cloud is apparent near the eastern Caribbean. The broad green tones dominating the Gulf of Mexico and Southeast U.S. confirm deep tropical moisture in place across that sector.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB Full Disk (GOES-19)
sources.summary: This GOES-19 Air Mass RGB from 04 September 2026 at 1320Z shows a well-organized tropical cyclone in the eastern Pacific west of the Baja California coast, displaying a clear cyclonic spiral with a tight, cold-topped center and banding features wrapping into it. A broad green airmass of tropical moisture extends across Central America, southern Mexico, and into the Caribbean, with scattered deep convective cells visible over the Yucatan Peninsula and the western Caribbean. Across Canada and into the Arctic, a sharp transition from deep blue-purple to red-orange marks a prominent airmass boundary consistent with the polar jet corridor, with the blue tones indicating cold, dry upper-tropospheric air poleward and the red-orange tones reflecting dry subsiding air on the equatorward flank. Over the North Atlantic northeast of the domain, a curved cloud structure suggests an extratropical cyclone, while across the South Atlantic and southern South America the red-orange coloring and thin cloud cover indicate dry, subsident upper-level conditions consistent with a mid-latitude ridge. Deep convection over the Amazon basin and northeastern Brazil appears as bright white cells embedded in a green moist background, suggesting active convective development along the South American monsoon region.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day Temperature Outlook
sources.summary: The most striking feature is a 90-100% probability bull's-eye for above-normal temperatures centered on Texas and Oklahoma, expanding outward to encompass essentially the entire southern tier from the Desert Southwest through the Gulf Coast states and Florida at the 70-80% level, and reaching the Great Lakes and mid-Atlantic at the 50-60% level. The only area holding out against the warm signal is the Pacific Northwest and northern Rockies, which fall in the near-normal gray category, suggesting that region sits under a different or weaker regime. New England also shows near-normal odds, consistent with the warm anomaly core being displaced well to the south and west of that corner of the country. The tight concentric probability gradient centered on the south-central Plains implies a persistent, positively tilted ridge axis over or near that region rather than a transient warm spell, since CPC outlooks at this range tend toward above-normal only when the large-scale pattern is expected to be stable through the valid period. Alaska shows a mixed signal — above-normal odds for the southern coast and Aleutian chain but near-normal for the interior — which is consistent with a broadly amplified pattern in that sector as well, though the two domains cannot be directly linked from this chart alone.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary: This is indeed a CPC 6-10 day 500 mb height and height anomaly forecast, valid 9-13 September 2026. The green contours show heights in decameters, with the innermost closed contour over the Canadian Arctic reading 528 dam, and ridging over the south-central contiguous US reaching approximately 588 dam near the Gulf Coast, consistent with a late-summer subtropical ridge. The dashed contours are height anomalies plotted at 60-dam intervals, which is almost certainly 6-dam intervals mislabeled or a rendering artifact — taking the labeled values at face value, the anomaly field shows a strong positive center of +90 dam labeled over the Canadian Arctic and a negative center of -60 dam over the eastern North Pacific, but anomalies of that magnitude are physically implausible for a 500 mb field; the most defensible reading is that the dashed contour interval is 6 dam (60 m), making the Arctic positive center roughly +90 units on that scale and the Pacific trough roughly -60 units, both of which are large but more plausible if the unit is actually meters rather than dam. The ridge axis over western North America runs roughly north-south near 100-105°W through the central Plains, and the zero anomaly line appears to lie near the Pacific coast, meaning positive anomalies do not extend significantly into the interior western US, suggesting the western ridge has retreated eastward and the flow over the Pacific is trending more zonal. A trough axis is implied by the height minimum centered over the Canadian Arctic Archipelago, with southward-dipping contours over the eastern North Pacific flanking the ridge to the west.

sources.title: CPC 8-14 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary: This chart is a 500 mb height and height-anomaly forecast valid 11–17 September 2026, made 3 September 2026, with green solid contours for heights (60 dam intervals) and blue/red dashed contours for anomalies. The dominant feature is a deep closed low centered over the Canadian Arctic Archipelago, with heights near 528 dam at the core; the surrounding anomaly contours show a strong negative center there, with the innermost blue dashed contour reading near –90 dam, which would be physically unreasonable for a 500 mb anomaly — this is almost certainly plotted in meters (roughly –9 dam), consistent with a moderately deep cold-core trough anomaly. Over western North America, the height pattern shows a broad, nearly zonal to slightly anticyclonic flow across the western contiguous U.S. and British Columbia, with the 570 dam contour arching across the southern Plains and the Southwest; there is no well-defined positive anomaly center over western Canada, the northern Rockies, or the northern Plains — the anomaly zero line (purple dashed) runs roughly through the interior West, indicating near-normal to slightly below-normal heights across that region, not a ridge centered there. The ridge axis implied by the height pattern is displaced well to the south, centered over the Desert Southwest and northern Mexico near 576–582 dam, meaning the northern Rockies and northern Plains fall on the equatorward flank of the circumpolar trough rather than under a positive anomaly ridge. A modest positive anomaly (red dashed, inner contour near +9 dam in meter-equivalent units) appears over the central and southern Plains near the Kansas–Oklahoma area, consistent with a weak downstream ridge building southeast of the main trough.

sources.title: WPC Short Range Forecast Discussion
sources.summary: Upper-level trough deepening over southeastern Canada will sustain strong to severe thunderstorms from upper Midwest to Mid-Atlantic through Friday-Saturday, gradually shifting southward. Cool air mass will advance into northeastern U.S., with temperatures dropping to 40s-50s by Sunday morning. Heat dome anchored over midsection persists through Labor Day weekend with widespread Heat Advisories and Extreme Heat Warnings; major to extreme heat risk expected. Monsoonal moisture across Arizona-New Mexico will trigger scattered thunderstorms and locally heavy rain through the weekend, with Slight Risk of excessive rainfall along Arizona-New Mexico border. Northwestern U.S. experiencing unsettled conditions with embedded thunderstorms. Gulf Coast region and Florida vulnerable to flash flooding from weak disturbances. Below-average temperatures and freezing elevations across the West.

sources.title: SPC Day 1 Convective Outlook
sources.summary: Slight risk of severe thunderstorms from southern Great Lakes through mid-Atlantic today into tonight. A cluster of thunderstorms moving southeast from the Upper Midwest will encounter diurnal instability across the Ohio Valley and mid-Atlantic, with ample low-level moisture and steep lapse rates supporting strong outflow winds. Best potential for damaging gusts in central and eastern Ohio where shear and buoyancy overlap favorably. Bowing line segments expected to dominate. Weak lee trough across central Plains may initiate convection with strong downdrafts possible, but convective inhibition and model height rises create uncertainty over whether storms will develop.

sources.title: SPC Mesoscale Discussions
sources.summary: Organizing convective cluster/MCS over eastern Wisconsin may intensify into an MCS capable of producing severe wind gusts (55-70 mph) and hail (up to 1.25 inches) as it crosses into lower Michigan and potentially Ohio/Indiana by morning. Low-level warm air advection and a 30-40 knot jet are supporting convective organization and cold pool strengthening. Moderate downstream instability and shear should maintain intensity. Primary uncertainty centers on whether the strongest gusts will reach the surface. Watch issuance considered possible but uncertain (40 percent probability).

sources.title: NHC Tropical Weather Outlooks
sources.summary:
Atlantic: No tropical cyclone formation expected over the next 7 days across the North Atlantic, Caribbean, or Gulf of America.

East Pacific: Three active hurricanes under NHC advisory—Karina east of Hawaii, Lowell south of Hawaii, and Marie southwest of Baja California. An area of low pressure well offshore southwestern Mexico may develop early next week, with medium chance (50 percent) of tropical depression formation by mid-week while tracking west-northwestward at 10-15 mph, expected to remain well offshore Mexico.

sources.title: ENSO State (Oceanic Niño Index)
sources.summary: The Oceanic Niño Index shows a transition from weak La Niña conditions currently (NDJ 2025 at -0.60 anomaly) toward El Niño by mid-2026. The phase crosses into neutral territory around February-March 2026, then strengthens into El Niño by April-May 2026. By summer 2026 (JJA), the anomaly reaches +1.80, indicating moderate El Niño conditions. The trend is consistently warming across the forecast period.

sources.title: Teleconnection Indices (PNA, AO, NAO)
sources.summary: PNA has weakened into negative territory, currently -0.17 with the 7-day mean at -0.70 and falling, suggesting reduced western ridge/eastern trough support. AO has swung sharply positive (current -0.35, 7-day mean +0.37, rising from -0.05), indicating a shift away from high-latitude blocking. NAO has deteriorated markedly to -1.28, with the 7-day mean at -0.90 and declining from +0.19, potentially affecting eastern North Atlantic weather escape routes. Note: these are summer indices with inherently weak canonical patterns; treat directionally only.
